medical.title: Infant mortality falls by 16% in some of England's most deprived areas, new national data show
medical.summary: Infant mortality in some of England's most disadvantaged areas fell by 16% from April 2025 to March 2026 compared with the previous year, according to the latest national data published by the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD) at the University of Bristol.

medical.title: Molecular mapping of 8 million cells brings cerebral architecture into focus
medical.summary: University of California, Irvine researchers have mapped approximately 8 million cells in regions deep within the human brain, identifying 60 distinct types and revealing how they form cellular communities. The work offers a foundational reference for investigating brain systems affected by Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

medical.title: Cancer vaccines show promise for treatment and prevention
medical.summary: For more than three decades, Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have pursued an ambitious idea: that vaccines could train the immune system to recognize and fight cancer. Now, a landmark phase 3 clinical trial of a personalized melanoma vaccine shows that this approach can improve outcomes for patients. Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center was among the clinical centers that participated in the multicenter study.

medical.title: Key brain area reveals distinct zones whose boundaries blur with age
medical.summary: Scientists in the Center for Human Brain Variation at the Broad Institute have charted previously hidden architecture and patterns of cellular makeup in a key part of the brain called the striatum, which is involved in decision-making and movement and is affected in psychiatric disorders, addiction and neurodegeneration. The findings reveal six new zones within the striatum based on gene expression patterns. They also demonstrate how the zones' boundaries blur with age and highlight ways that advancing age and genetic variation affect gene expression in the brain.

medical.title: Personalized mobile health coaching offers new approach to preventing gestational diabetes in high-risk pregnancies
medical.summary: A continuous, personalized mobile health (mHealth) coaching program can significantly reduce gestational diabetes incidence among high-risk pregnant women, independent of changes to maternal weight—according to an international study published in the Lancet Digital Health.

medical.title: Organ-on-chip shows how tumors interact with nerves and blood vessels
medical.summary: On an organ-on-a-chip, researchers can now explore how tumors grow and interact with their surroundings. The chip, a small plate where cancer cells, nerves and blood vessels grow, was developed by researchers at Linköping University, Sweden, in collaboration with colleagues at Politecnico di Milano in Italy. It is described in an article published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: AI-powered lung cancer atlas identifies cell types linked to higher risk of spread
medical.summary: Recent advances in cancer biology have shown that a tumor is not a uniform mass. It consists of many different cancer cells and is embedded in an environment of immune cells, connective tissue and blood vessels. This variety is a significant factor in determining whether a tumor spreads and how well a therapy works. While single-cell approaches are considered pioneering instruments in cancer research, their translation into clinical practice has been limited to date, primarily due to a lack of large patient data sets with comprehensive clinical histories.

medical.title: What spaceflight reveals about nerves and bone recovery
medical.summary: Mechanical loading is important for maintaining bone mass, and researchers from Science Tokyo have found that sensory nerves inside the bone play a key role in this process. In mice, sensory nerve abundance changed in response to mechanical unloading and reloading, and removing these nerves prevented bone recovery. The findings reveal a link between mechanical loading, sensory nerves and bone recovery and could support sensory nerve-targeted therapies and rehabilitation strategies for osteoporosis and fragility.

medical.title: A novel pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome induced by direct stimulation of Ephrin-B1
medical.summary: A group led by the Department of Cell Biology at the Kidney Research Center, Niigata University, has identified a novel Ca²⁺-independent pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome. The study is published in The American Journal of Pathology.

medical.title: Once considered junk, cellular 'chimeras' emerge as key to better cancer care
medical.summary: UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have found an answer to one of the great mysteries of human biology, and the discovery could have major implications for the battle against breast cancer and other diseases.

medical.title: Pilot study tests cell therapy for difficult-to-heal diabetic foot ulcers
medical.summary: An experimental cell therapy was well tolerated in 10 people with chronic diabetic foot ulcers, according to a first-in-human study led by researchers at Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine (WFIRM).

medical.title: Rethinking the road to cancer care in Rwanda
medical.summary: While studying health systems around the world during a yearlong fellowship, Abel Sapirstein traveled to northern Rwanda to visit Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence, which at the time was the country's only publicly accessible facility to offer comprehensive oncology services.

medical.title: Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
medical.summary: Scientists are calling for a major rethink of how we manage high blood pressure, suggesting that eating more potassium could be just as important as cutting back on salt. A new report finds that combining increased potassium intake with reduced sodium consumption may offer greater benefits for blood pressure control than sodium reduction alone.

medical.title: New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss
medical.summary: Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.

medical.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
medical.summary: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.

medical.title: Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep
medical.summary: A major new review challenges the growing enthusiasm for medical cannabis as an insomnia treatment, finding little reliable evidence that it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or daytime functioning. Researchers caution that this doesn't mean cannabis is ineffective, only that existing studies are too weak to establish whether it works.

science.title: Black rhinos are mostly loners, but not always: Why this matters for saving the species
science.summary: Black rhinos are notoriously aggressive, not just to humans but also to their fellow black rhinos. Aggression is so prevalent that injuries sustained after fighting with another black rhino are a common cause of death. Because of this aggression and their solitary nature, black rhino social behavior has been largely unexplored. Yet it may be key to conservation of this critically endangered African icon.

science.title: Early signs of stock market instability may appear in how traders place orders
science.summary: The influence of financial markets cannot be overstated, and this influence highlights the need for thorough market analysis. However, being thorough can be difficult when markets are highly complex and ever-changing, prompting the search for a suitable approach to analysis. Fortunately, the increasing availability of detailed market data, together with advances in mathematical theories, offers new opportunities to better understand market behavior.

science.title: Magnetic nanoparticles cut adhesive curing from 24 hours to one in laboratory tests
science.summary: Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) and global automotive supplier Motherson are collaborating to develop a magnetic heating technology that could significantly reduce the time and energy needed to cure industrial coatings.

science.title: Robotic tools help unlock the hidden microbial world of the deep sea
science.summary: Scientists have developed a robotic system that can recreate the extreme conditions of the deep ocean in the laboratory, opening up access to some microorganisms for the first time.

science.title: Using AI to predict how bioplastics behave under heat
science.summary: A new ANIPH study shows how machine learning models can predict how PHB and PHBV respond to heat, helping manufacturers design formulations that are easier to process.

science.title: Not afraid of ghosts: Curiosity and fearlessness apparent in German shepherd genes
science.summary: German shepherd dogs bred for working are more curious and less neurotic than German shepherds bred for show. A new study from Uppsala University and the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences has shown that the differences are not only apparent in the dogs' behavior, but also in their genes. In previous studies, similar genes in humans have been associated with neuroticism. The research is published in the journal Animal Genetics.

science.title: Global climate policies continue to advance despite setbacks, research finds
science.summary: The latest findings from the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor, led by the Blavatnik School of Government and the Oxford Sustainable Law Programme, show that progress in Asia, Africa and Latin America is more than offsetting the weakening or reversal of climate policies in parts of Europe and North America.

science.title: Product for controlling agricultural pests proves harmful to iconic banana slug
science.summary: Researchers at Oregon State University say a product used to control pest slugs on farms in multiple countries is harmful to an iconic West Coast slug and that more research is needed before the product is approved for use in the United States. The work is published in the journal PLOS One.

science.title: Unknowns play a major role in mortgage foreclosure decisions
science.summary: When it comes to making decisions regarding mortgage foreclosures, a bank doesn't know what it doesn't know.

science.title: Multiplexed detector system precisely counts more than 9,000 photons
science.summary: Researchers have developed a new approach that can precisely count from zero to more than 9,000 individual photons. The advance opens new possibilities for studying quantum light at large scales and making precise optical measurements.

science.title: Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought
science.summary: How does climate change affect the East Asian monsoon? Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment.

science.title: Matter–antimatter asymmetry still provides no evidence of new physics
science.summary: The universe's dominance by ordinary matter is compelling evidence that matter and antimatter are not perfect reflections of each other. However, known differences do not explain the scale of this imbalance, leaving open the possibility that unknown physics is responsible. A new analysis of meson decays, conducted by the LHCb collaboration, has narrowed the scope of the search for such a scenario while paving the way for more precise measurements in the future.

science.title: Chip-based laser cooling could ease quantum computing bottleneck
science.summary: Researchers at Cornell have developed a laser-cooling technique that could potentially remove a significant bottleneck in the development of larger, faster quantum computers.

science.title: Europe's look-alike Alpine newts turn out to be five distinct species
science.summary: What scientists until recently called the Alpine newt has turned out to be five different species, following genetic research by Leiden biologists. One of these species was even new to science and has now been given a name: Mesotriton similis.

science.title: Mapping oxygen in graphene oxide could unlock better materials
science.summary: Just one atom thick, graphene is the thinnest and strongest material ever measured. It can also conduct electricity and heat extremely well. These remarkable properties have generated interest in using graphene in everything from solar cells and batteries to water filters and sensors. Turning those possibilities into practical technologies, however, requires scientists to understand how changes to graphene's structure affect the way it behaves.

science.title: Engineering team creates 3D-printed raptor puppets to help wildlife rehabilitation
science.summary: Four new feeding puppets at Salthaven Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Centre will help caregivers feed young raptors while reducing their contact with people when baby season returns next year.

science.title: Uncovering the hidden origins of the placenta
science.summary: When an embryo attaches to the wall of the uterus roughly six days after fertilization, it begins to build the body and placenta. Called implantation, this is the stage of life scientists know least about. It is also the stage when most pregnancies are lost.

science.title: Catalyst regeneration enables durable hydrogen production from ammonia
science.summary: Researchers at the National University of Singapore (NUS) have developed a catalyst-regeneration strategy that could make hydrogen production from ammonia more efficient and reliable. By tackling a major problem that causes catalysts to lose their effectiveness over time, the team sustained hydrogen production for over 2,000 hours in laboratory tests.

science.title: Layered superionic conductor hosts atomic vibrations that behave like liquids, glasses and crystals
science.summary: Scientists from the Institute of Metal Research (IMR) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have directly observed liquid-like, glass-like and crystal-like phonon behaviors coexisting in a crystalline solid—the layered superionic conductor AgCrSe₂.

environment.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
environment.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

environment.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
environment.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

environment.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
environment.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

environment.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
environment.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

environment.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
environment.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

environment.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
environment.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco
mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Black rhinos are mostly loners, but not always: Why this matters for saving the species
mix_items.summary: Black rhinos are notoriously aggressive, not just to humans but also to their fellow black rhinos. Aggression is so prevalent that injuries sustained after fighting with another black rhino are a common cause of death. Because of this aggression and their solitary nature, black rhino social behavior has been largely unexplored. Yet it may be key to conservation of this critically endangered African icon.

mix_items.title: Infant mortality falls by 16% in some of England's most deprived areas, new national data show
mix_items.summary: Infant mortality in some of England's most disadvantaged areas fell by 16% from April 2025 to March 2026 compared with the previous year, according to the latest national data published by the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD) at the University of Bristol.

mix_items.title: Early signs of stock market instability may appear in how traders place orders
mix_items.summary: The influence of financial markets cannot be overstated, and this influence highlights the need for thorough market analysis. However, being thorough can be difficult when markets are highly complex and ever-changing, prompting the search for a suitable approach to analysis. Fortunately, the increasing availability of detailed market data, together with advances in mathematical theories, offers new opportunities to better understand market behavior.

mix_items.title: Molecular mapping of 8 million cells brings cerebral architecture into focus
mix_items.summary: University of California, Irvine researchers have mapped approximately 8 million cells in regions deep within the human brain, identifying 60 distinct types and revealing how they form cellular communities. The work offers a foundational reference for investigating brain systems affected by Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease and other neurological and psychiatric disorders.

mix_items.title: Magnetic nanoparticles cut adhesive curing from 24 hours to one in laboratory tests
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) and global automotive supplier Motherson are collaborating to develop a magnetic heating technology that could significantly reduce the time and energy needed to cure industrial coatings.

mix_items.title: Cancer vaccines show promise for treatment and prevention
mix_items.summary: For more than three decades, Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have pursued an ambitious idea: that vaccines could train the immune system to recognize and fight cancer. Now, a landmark phase 3 clinical trial of a personalized melanoma vaccine shows that this approach can improve outcomes for patients. Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center was among the clinical centers that participated in the multicenter study.

mix_items.title: Robotic tools help unlock the hidden microbial world of the deep sea
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed a robotic system that can recreate the extreme conditions of the deep ocean in the laboratory, opening up access to some microorganisms for the first time.

mix_items.title: Key brain area reveals distinct zones whose boundaries blur with age
mix_items.summary: Scientists in the Center for Human Brain Variation at the Broad Institute have charted previously hidden architecture and patterns of cellular makeup in a key part of the brain called the striatum, which is involved in decision-making and movement and is affected in psychiatric disorders, addiction and neurodegeneration. The findings reveal six new zones within the striatum based on gene expression patterns. They also demonstrate how the zones' boundaries blur with age and highlight ways that advancing age and genetic variation affect gene expression in the brain.

mix_items.title: Using AI to predict how bioplastics behave under heat
mix_items.summary: A new ANIPH study shows how machine learning models can predict how PHB and PHBV respond to heat, helping manufacturers design formulations that are easier to process.

mix_items.title: Not afraid of ghosts: Curiosity and fearlessness apparent in German shepherd genes
mix_items.summary: German shepherd dogs bred for working are more curious and less neurotic than German shepherds bred for show. A new study from Uppsala University and the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences has shown that the differences are not only apparent in the dogs' behavior, but also in their genes. In previous studies, similar genes in humans have been associated with neuroticism. The research is published in the journal Animal Genetics.

mix_items.title: Global climate policies continue to advance despite setbacks, research finds
mix_items.summary: The latest findings from the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor, led by the Blavatnik School of Government and the Oxford Sustainable Law Programme, show that progress in Asia, Africa and Latin America is more than offsetting the weakening or reversal of climate policies in parts of Europe and North America.

mix_items.title: Product for controlling agricultural pests proves harmful to iconic banana slug
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Oregon State University say a product used to control pest slugs on farms in multiple countries is harmful to an iconic West Coast slug and that more research is needed before the product is approved for use in the United States. The work is published in the journal PLOS One.

mix_items.title: Unknowns play a major role in mortgage foreclosure decisions
mix_items.summary: When it comes to making decisions regarding mortgage foreclosures, a bank doesn't know what it doesn't know.

mix_items.title: Personalized mobile health coaching offers new approach to preventing gestational diabetes in high-risk pregnancies
mix_items.summary: A continuous, personalized mobile health (mHealth) coaching program can significantly reduce gestational diabetes incidence among high-risk pregnant women, independent of changes to maternal weight—according to an international study published in the Lancet Digital Health.

mix_items.title: Multiplexed detector system precisely counts more than 9,000 photons
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed a new approach that can precisely count from zero to more than 9,000 individual photons. The advance opens new possibilities for studying quantum light at large scales and making precise optical measurements.

mix_items.title: Organ-on-chip shows how tumors interact with nerves and blood vessels
mix_items.summary: On an organ-on-a-chip, researchers can now explore how tumors grow and interact with their surroundings. The chip, a small plate where cancer cells, nerves and blood vessels grow, was developed by researchers at Linköping University, Sweden, in collaboration with colleagues at Politecnico di Milano in Italy. It is described in an article published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought
mix_items.summary: How does climate change affect the East Asian monsoon? Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment.

mix_items.title: Matter–antimatter asymmetry still provides no evidence of new physics
mix_items.summary: The universe's dominance by ordinary matter is compelling evidence that matter and antimatter are not perfect reflections of each other. However, known differences do not explain the scale of this imbalance, leaving open the possibility that unknown physics is responsible. A new analysis of meson decays, conducted by the LHCb collaboration, has narrowed the scope of the search for such a scenario while paving the way for more precise measurements in the future.

mix_items.title: AI-powered lung cancer atlas identifies cell types linked to higher risk of spread
mix_items.summary: Recent advances in cancer biology have shown that a tumor is not a uniform mass. It consists of many different cancer cells and is embedded in an environment of immune cells, connective tissue and blood vessels. This variety is a significant factor in determining whether a tumor spreads and how well a therapy works. While single-cell approaches are considered pioneering instruments in cancer research, their translation into clinical practice has been limited to date, primarily due to a lack of large patient data sets with comprehensive clinical histories.

mix_items.title: Chip-based laser cooling could ease quantum computing bottleneck
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Cornell have developed a laser-cooling technique that could potentially remove a significant bottleneck in the development of larger, faster quantum computers.

mix_items.title: What spaceflight reveals about nerves and bone recovery
mix_items.summary: Mechanical loading is important for maintaining bone mass, and researchers from Science Tokyo have found that sensory nerves inside the bone play a key role in this process. In mice, sensory nerve abundance changed in response to mechanical unloading and reloading, and removing these nerves prevented bone recovery. The findings reveal a link between mechanical loading, sensory nerves and bone recovery and could support sensory nerve-targeted therapies and rehabilitation strategies for osteoporosis and fragility.

mix_items.title: Europe's look-alike Alpine newts turn out to be five distinct species
mix_items.summary: What scientists until recently called the Alpine newt has turned out to be five different species, following genetic research by Leiden biologists. One of these species was even new to science and has now been given a name: Mesotriton similis.

mix_items.title: Mapping oxygen in graphene oxide could unlock better materials
mix_items.summary: Just one atom thick, graphene is the thinnest and strongest material ever measured. It can also conduct electricity and heat extremely well. These remarkable properties have generated interest in using graphene in everything from solar cells and batteries to water filters and sensors. Turning those possibilities into practical technologies, however, requires scientists to understand how changes to graphene's structure affect the way it behaves.

mix_items.title: Engineering team creates 3D-printed raptor puppets to help wildlife rehabilitation
mix_items.summary: Four new feeding puppets at Salthaven Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Centre will help caregivers feed young raptors while reducing their contact with people when baby season returns next year.

mix_items.title: A novel pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome induced by direct stimulation of Ephrin-B1
mix_items.summary: A group led by the Department of Cell Biology at the Kidney Research Center, Niigata University, has identified a novel Ca²⁺-independent pathogenic mechanism of nephrotic syndrome. The study is published in The American Journal of Pathology.

mix_items.title: Once considered junk, cellular 'chimeras' emerge as key to better cancer care
mix_items.summary: UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center researchers have found an answer to one of the great mysteries of human biology, and the discovery could have major implications for the battle against breast cancer and other diseases.

mix_items.title: Uncovering the hidden origins of the placenta
mix_items.summary: When an embryo attaches to the wall of the uterus roughly six days after fertilization, it begins to build the body and placenta. Called implantation, this is the stage of life scientists know least about. It is also the stage when most pregnancies are lost.

mix_items.title: Catalyst regeneration enables durable hydrogen production from ammonia
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the National University of Singapore (NUS) have developed a catalyst-regeneration strategy that could make hydrogen production from ammonia more efficient and reliable. By tackling a major problem that causes catalysts to lose their effectiveness over time, the team sustained hydrogen production for over 2,000 hours in laboratory tests.

mix_items.title: Layered superionic conductor hosts atomic vibrations that behave like liquids, glasses and crystals
mix_items.summary: Scientists from the Institute of Metal Research (IMR) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have directly observed liquid-like, glass-like and crystal-like phonon behaviors coexisting in a crystalline solid—the layered superionic conductor AgCrSe₂.

mix_items.title: Pilot study tests cell therapy for difficult-to-heal diabetic foot ulcers
mix_items.summary: An experimental cell therapy was well tolerated in 10 people with chronic diabetic foot ulcers, according to a first-in-human study led by researchers at Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine (WFIRM).

mix_items.title: Rethinking the road to cancer care in Rwanda
mix_items.summary: While studying health systems around the world during a yearlong fellowship, Abel Sapirstein traveled to northern Rwanda to visit Butaro Cancer Center of Excellence, which at the time was the country's only publicly accessible facility to offer comprehensive oncology services.

mix_items.title: US companies apply to explore deep-sea mining in area bordering Pacific island states
mix_items.summary: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back. The applications are part of a broader move by U.S. companies to […]

mix_items.title: What do a bean and a flamingo have in common? Finding the unexpected in nature photos
mix_items.summary: Photographer Andrew Zuckerman took a moment longer than usual to look closely at a bean that was sprouting in his studio. “There was this one bean that sort of had this incredibly elegant curve, and I thought, ‘God, that’s exactly like the flamingo from like 15 years ago,’” Zuckerman tells Mongabay in a video call. […]

mix_items.title: Angolan hunters protect Southern Africa’s internationally important wetland
mix_items.summary: Four years ago, elders from several different communities in Angola’s southeastern highlands approached environmental anthropologist Kerllen Costa, saying they’d noticed an influx of people from outside the highlands coming there to hunt for bushmeat without obtaining permission from local chiefs. Sometimes the outsiders recruited locals to hunt on their behalf. These hunting parties were disregarding […]

mix_items.title: US brand StarKist suspends tuna sourcing from vessels accused of exploiting Indonesian fishers
mix_items.summary: U.S. tuna brand StarKist has announced a halt on purchases from fishing vessels linked to forced labor practices in a recent report. It also says it has hired an outside firm to investigate after an Indonesian migrant fishers’ union demanded a binding labor agreement with the company. In a statement sent to Mongabay on Nov. […]

mix_items.title: Weird and wonderful wildlife revealed in underexplored mountains
mix_items.summary: A long-term camera trap study has uncovered a treasure trove of wildlife in the Annamite mountains, that run through Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. The mountains have been called the “Amazon of Asia” owing to the huge variety of species here. With hunting and tree loss threatening the area, conservationists are racing to formulate a plan […]

mix_items.title: Investigation continues in Indonesia after first conviction in 3-ton pangolin trafficking case
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesian investigators say they expect further developments in a major wildlife trafficking case after an intermediary was sentenced to nine years in prison over the discovery of 3.05 metric tons of pangolin scales at the country’s largest port in February this year. “We’re continuing to expand the investigation to dismantle this illegal […]

mix_items.title: Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
mix_items.summary: Scientists are calling for a major rethink of how we manage high blood pressure, suggesting that eating more potassium could be just as important as cutting back on salt. A new report finds that combining increased potassium intake with reduced sodium consumption may offer greater benefits for blood pressure control than sodium reduction alone.

mix_items.title: New diabetes implant uses electricity to lower blood sugar and promote weight loss
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed a remarkable new electronic implant that could transform type 2 diabetes treatment by lowering blood sugar without insulin or traditional drugs. The device uses a special electrically powered catalyst to convert excess glucose into a substance that the body eliminates through urine, potentially preventing unwanted energy from being stored as fat. In diabetic mice, the implant precisely controlled blood sugar and promoted weight loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
mix_items.summary: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.

mix_items.title: Scientists find surprisingly little evidence that medical cannabis helps you sleep
mix_items.summary: A major new review challenges the growing enthusiasm for medical cannabis as an insomnia treatment, finding little reliable evidence that it improves sleep quality, sleep duration, or daytime functioning. Researchers caution that this doesn't mean cannabis is ineffective, only that existing studies are too weak to establish whether it works.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
